title: Theater and Virtual Set Design
answer: Stage renderings, projection mapping, lighting plots, costume synthesis and acoustic modelling.

children.name: Stage Design and Architectural Rendering
children.blurb: Stage design and architectural rendering covers the work of turning a script, a brief or a concept into spatial images that a director, a producer or a client can read and approve.

children.name: Projection Mapping and Generative Backdrops
children.blurb: Projection mapping and generative backdrops cover the use of software to paint light onto physical surfaces and to produce moving imagery behind performers.

children.name: Lighting Plots and Cue Design
children.blurb: Lighting plots and cue design cover the documents and decisions that fix where light comes from, what it falls on, and when it changes during a performance or a shoot.

children.name: Costume Concept and Fabric Simulation
children.blurb: Costume concept and fabric simulation covers the work of turning a character brief into a wearable design and then predicting how cloth will behave on a body in motion.

children.name: Acoustic Modelling for Sets
children.blurb: Acoustic modelling for sets covers the prediction and shaping of how sound behaves inside a built or virtual environment, from a single room to a full stage.

sections.body: Artificial intelligence in theater and virtual set design covers the tools and methods used to plan, visualize and build stages, whether the audience is in a physical auditorium or watching through a camera. In practice, generative image models turn a director's description into concept renderings of a set, and 3D reconstruction pipelines convert sketches or photographs into walkable digital models that a creative team can revise before anything is built. Projection systems use generative backdrops that respond to actor movement, and machine learning assists with lighting by proposing cue timing and color palettes from a script or a rehearsal recording. Costume work uses fabric simulation to predict how cloth drapes and moves, and acoustic modelling predicts how sound behaves in a proposed room or set configuration. None of this replaces the designer. It compresses the iteration loop between an idea and something a collaborator can see, hear or stand inside.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven across these areas. Architectural rendering and fabric simulation are relatively mature, because the underlying physics and graphics problems are well studied and the outputs are checked by eye. Projection mapping is reliable when the geometry is fixed and the content is pre-rendered, but live tracking of performers on a busy stage still fails in cluttered scenes, under difficult lighting, or when costumes and props occlude markers. Lighting cue design has useful assistive tools, yet automated plots rarely account for the full intent of a scene, and designers treat suggestions as drafts rather than decisions. Acoustic modelling is strong for prediction in known spaces and weaker when a set is temporary, irregular or full of absorbent materials that were never measured. The honest limits are shared: these systems need good input data, they produce plausible rather than correct results, and every output still requires a human with theatrical judgment to accept, reject or repair it.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here follow the production sequence from empty space to finished performance. Stage Design and Architectural Rendering is the starting point, covering how a script or brief becomes a spatial concept and how AI-assisted modelling helps a team test scale, sightlines and buildability. Projection Mapping and Generative Backdrops then takes that space and asks what appears on its surfaces, including the tracking and calibration problems that decide whether a backdrop feels alive or merely projected. Lighting Plots and Cue Design sits alongside it, dealing with the timing, color and intensity decisions that shape mood and focus, and with how much of that work can be proposed automatically. Costume Concept and Fabric Simulation moves to the performer, covering design ideation and the physics of how garments behave in motion. Acoustic Modelling for Sets closes the loop by treating the set as a sounding object, predicting how speech, music and effects will carry in the room that the other pages have designed.
